pattern: ML model deployment requires explicit serving infrastructure: models are not files but services with versioning, routing, and gradual rollout capabilities. Key patterns: (1) Model registry — single source of truth for model artifacts with metadata (metrics, dataset versions, training params); (2) Can ary/AB deployment — route small traffic % to new model, compare performance before full rollout; (3) Shadow mode — run new model alongside production without affecting user experience; (4) Feature stores — consistent feature computation between training and serving to prevent train/serving skew. Key insight: the hardest part of ML is not training but deploying reliably — a perfect model that never reaches production has zero value.

description: ML observability spans four orthogonal dimensions: (1) Experiment tracking — capture hyperparameters, metrics, artifacts per run with lineage (MLflow/W&B); (2) Data drift detection — monitor feature distribution shifts over time with statistical tests (KS test, PSI); (3) Model performance monitoring — track prediction distributions, latency, error rates in production; (4) Feature stores — centralized serving layer for consistent train/serving features (Feast, Tecton). Key pattern: observability must be automatic, not opt-in. Manual instrumentation creates blind spots. The model serving layer emits telemetry; the observability layer ingests and correlates. Drift detection should run continuously, not just at retrain triggers.
source: Synthesized from MLflow, Weights & Biases, Arize, WhyLabs documentation
